items.title: August CPI shows sticky core inflation ahead of Fed meeting
items.description: An interest rate hike may be in store after data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics , released on Friday, shows that core inflation is remaining stubbornly above the Federal Reserve’s desired target. In August, the Consumer Price Index for all items rose 0.4% month-over-month up from a 0.1% monthly jump in July. A 3.9% month-over-month jump in the index for gasoline contributed to over one-third of the monthly all items index increase. Overall, the energy index rose 2.1% month-over-month in August. “Inflation regained momentum in August, with higher energy prices lifting the headline rate and stubborn services prices keeping underlying inflation pressures alive,” Sam Williamson, First American ’s senior economist, said in a statement. On a yearly basis, inflation was up 3.4% in August, the same as in July. Core inflation, also known as the all items less food and energy index, rose 0.3% in August after a 0.2% monthly increase in July. On a year-over-year basis, the all items less food and energy index rose 2.4%, down from a 2.5% jump in July. Indexes that contributed to the monthly jump of the all items less food and energy index include communication (+2.3%), airline fares (+2.7%), education (+0.8%) and used cars and trucks (+0.4%). On the other hand, the indexes for medical care (-0.2%) and motor vehicle insurance (-0.8%) decreased in August. “The firmer monthly reading and persistent services inflation show that underlying price pressures remain stubborn,” Williamson said. Month-over-month, the index for food jumped 0.1%, while the index for energy posted a 2.1% increase. On a yearly basis, the index for food rose 2.7%, while the index for energy rose 16.3%, largely in part due to a 27.4% annual increase in the gasoline index. The index for shelter rose 3.0% over the past year and 0.3% month-over-month in August. Owners’ equivalent rent of residence rose 3.1% year-over-year and 0.2% month-over-month. Overall, Williamson feels that the firmer core inflation reading puts another thumb on the scale toward a potential interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve at its meeting next week . “With the labor market still on solid footing, policymakers have room to lean harder against inflation. That would likely keep borrowing costs elevated in the near term as markets price in a higher path for interest rates,” he said. “For homebuyers, the path to lower mortgage rates still runs through lower inflation. Over time, more restrictive policy may help by convincing investors that inflation will come back under control, but meaningful rate relief remains out of reach for now. For now, rising incomes and cooling house prices are still helping buyers slowly regain some purchasing power, but borrowing costs are still pulling harder in the affordability tug of war.” Related More: Federal Reserve Inflation Interest Rates

items.title: Putting the ROAD Act into action faces a funding and HUD gauntlet
items.description: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law two months ago . Now comes the hard part: getting the money to get the results. The implementation process, including securing funding for new programs and finalizing regulatory changes, could take from now until well into 2028, optimistically speaking. After that, possibly, some early outcomes. The bill, the most comprehensive federal housing legislation in decades, includes a host of provisions to boost housing supply, including significant measures focused on attainable and affordable housing. While industry leaders almost unanimously applauded the bill’s passage, stakeholders acknowledge that implementing its provisions and the benefits that they would trigger will take time. Against this backdrop, a session hosted this week by the Bipartisan Policy Center and the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders (NAAHL) offered insights into roadblocks that could delay the implementation of certain provisions meant to increase the supply of attainable and affordable housing. While some supply-focused changes could have an impact quickly, others may take a year or more to begin to materialize. Why ROAD will take time to fund and implement ROAD created roughly a dozen new programs that require funding approval from Congress, a process typically painstaking, contentious and plodding. While some deadlines begin this year, many of the law’s new programs may hit delays because of a lack of federal funding. The House’s FY 2027 Transportation, Housing and Urban Development appropriations bill, which passed in June before ROAD became law, does not fund the ROAD provisions. The Senate appropriations bill is still pending, and it’s not yet clear if it will fund any of the programs tied to the housing legislation. “The Senate has not yet released its own funding bill, but it’s possible that many of the programs authorized in ROAD will not receive funding until fiscal year 2028 at the earliest,” Kristen Klurfield, associate director at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said during the session. Aaron Shroyer, Director of Policy and Advocacy at NAAHL, added that “until those programs get funded, they really only exist on paper.” The bill also changed regulations and public reporting requirements that federal agencies, most notably HUD, must implement. Federal agencies must write rules, issue guidance, establish programs and complete significant administrative work before provisions in the law can begin having their intended impact. HUD accounts for roughly 70% of the 125 identified federal actions and must develop nine new rulemakings. Because HUD rules typically take 18 months to two years to finalize, some rules in ROAD could be finalized in early 2028, though existing agency workloads could push that timeline further out. One wildcard is HUD’s staffing levels. The agency currently has about 5,800 employees , compared with 8,800 during fiscal year 2024, a 34% decrease in staffing. Some industry leaders worry that, with fewer workers, fully implementing the first comprehensive housing bill in decades could take years. “One of the biggest tasks for them at HUD and for other agencies is to figure out how to stack up these new rulemakings they’re tasked with against what was in their queue before ROAD,” Shroyer said. Manufactured housing’s permanent chassis removal A new rule that will remove the permanent chassis requirement from HUD’s manufactured housing definition is, potentially, one of the most consequential changes in the housing bill. The change will give manufacturers greater design flexibility to go vertical, enabling lower-cost manufactured housing to be built in high-density urban and infill markets, where manufactured homes are still uncommon. items.title: Office Revenues Are Failing To Keep Pace With Expenses
items.description: Office Revenues Are Failing To Keep Pace With Expenses September 11, 2026 | 4:27 pm ET Sasha Jones, New York City Despite office vacancy falling in most major cities , most landlords are still watching their margins shrink a half-decade after tenants embraced remote work. Median total operating expense growth has exceeded revenue every year from 2021 through 2025, according to a Trepp analysis of office properties backing CMBS loans. Unsplash/kate.sade Operating expenses have increased 2.7% annually, compared with a 1.3% growth rate for revenues. Net operating income has been squeezed to just a 0.2% uptick annually as a result. Overall, the implied five-year growth rate is 14.3% for operating expenses and 6.7% for revenues. NOI was up just 1% during the period, according to Trepp’s model. Trepp’s methodology involves matching properties year-to-year. The sample began with 3,599 properties in 2021 but declined to 2,266 in 2026. A property may exit the sample if it stops reporting, no longer has all of the financial metrics required to be included, is paid off, liquidated, or is taken over by a lender. Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio and Wisconsin have struggled the most, with NOI dropping by 1.4% over the five-year span. Also in the negatives were the West South Central states — containing Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas — and New England. NOI decreased by 0.5% and 0.1% for the respective regions. Property insurance has become the highest-growing expense across the board, rising a median 6.1% annually and 34.6% over the five years. In the Pacific U.S., insurance costs surged the most, with an annual median increase of 9.2%. The Middle and South Atlantic regions experienced the lowest increase at 4.6%. Utilities were the second-leading cost driver, increasing 4.9% annually and 27.1% between 2021 and 2025. Not included are the capital expenditures that office owners have had to shell out to upgrade their properties. Trophy buildings have attracted the greatest amount of leasing activity as companies use amenities and shorter commutes to draw employees back to in-person work . In markets like New York, where Class-A space has become hard to find — and afford — leasing has spilled over to Class-B properties. Still, many landlords find themselves needing to spend money to make money. But that spending adds to already growing maintenance and management costs. Each year between 2021 and 2025, building repairs increased 3.2%, payroll and benefits grew by 3.3%, administrative costs rose 2.7%, and management fees were up 1.3%. Trepp’s report notes that, looking forward, operating expense growth has moderated, but revenue growth has also slowed. In 2025, annual NOI growth was negative for the second consecutive year.
